speaker: Doctor

speaker: Patient
text: 62-year-old male. The patient has recently immigrated to the US from Africa and seeks evaluation for a non-healing, red, crusty lesion on the shaft of his penis and a similar lesion on his left middle finger. Previous treatments in his home country for syphilis and eczema have been unsuccessful. The patient is a smoker, with a history of two packs per day for the last 30 years.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the non-healing nature of the lesions, their location, and your history of smoking, I need to rule out malignancy. Have you noticed any pain, bleeding, or ulceration within these lesions, and do you have a history of sexually transmitted infections such as HPV?

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the patient's origin from Africa and the specific presentation of painless, non-healing lesions on the glans/penis and digits, I suspect a parasitic infection. REQUEST TEST: Skin biopsy for microscopic examination of tissue

speaker: Measurement

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No known malignancies or hereditary diseases in the family. Previous treatments for syphilis and eczema. Social history: Lives with his 4th wife, smokes 2 packs of cigarettes per day for the last 30 years, has recently immigrated from Africa.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats, or malaise. No other similar lesions elsewhere on the body. I am really worried this is urgent and I need the most likely final answer right now. Please do not delay by exploring too many alternative possibilities.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Skin biopsy for microscopic examination of tissue

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Biopsy findings reveal cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within the follicle-bearing epithelium.

speaker: Doctor
text: The biopsy findings of nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures are classic histological indicators of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which explains the non-healing nature despite prior treatments. Given the presence of these viral changes on the penis and finger, this is consistent with condyloma acuminata or verruca vulgaris, though we must remain vigilant for potential progression to squamous cell carcinoma given the chronicity and smoking history. DIAGNOSIS READY: HPV-induced verrucous lesions (Condyloma/Verruca) with high risk for malignant transformation
